lesson.title: The Fullness Signal: How Leptin Tells the Brain to Stop Eating
lesson.summary: Leptin is a hormone released by the body's fat cells that signals the hypothalamus when energy stores are sufficient, helping to suppress appetite and regulate body weight over the long term. When that signal fails to get through, as in leptin resistance, the brain can behave as though the body is starving even when it is not.
lesson.body:
Adrenaline, covered in the previous chapter, shows the endocrine system responding within seconds to an immediate threat. Leptin operates on the opposite end of the timescale, functioning as a slow, big picture signal of the body's overall energy reserves rather than a moment to moment cue. Leptin is released by adipose tissue, the body's fat cells, in amounts roughly proportional to how much fat is currently stored, which means it effectively reports back to the brain on the state of the body's longer term energy budget.

Leptin travels through the bloodstream, in keeping with the endocrine framework described earlier, and reaches the hypothalamus, where it binds receptors on neurons that regulate appetite and energy expenditure. Higher fat stores produce higher circulating leptin levels, and higher leptin levels signal the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure. In principle, this arrangement functions something like a thermostat, nudging body weight back toward a fairly stable range over the long run by discouraging further eating once reserves are adequate.

In practice, this system does not always work as smoothly as the simple thermostat model suggests. In many cases of obesity, leptin levels are already high, which makes sense given the larger fat stores involved, but the hypothalamus becomes less responsive to that signal, a state known as leptin resistance. Because the brain is not effectively receiving the message despite plenty of leptin circulating in the blood, it can end up behaving as though the body is underfed, continuing to drive hunger and conserve energy even when fat stores are already ample. This helps explain why obesity is not simply a matter of willpower: the underlying signaling system meant to regulate appetite can itself become disrupted.

One of the clearest illustrations of leptin's role comes from rare cases of genetic leptin deficiency, first documented in animal studies and later identified in a small number of human patients, in which the body is unable to produce leptin at all. Without any leptin reaching the hypothalamus, the brain never receives a satiety signal no matter how much fat is stored, resulting in severe, early onset obesity driven by persistent, unrelenting hunger. When these specific patients are given injections of synthetic leptin, appetite and weight can normalize dramatically, a striking natural experiment that helped confirm leptin's direct causal role in appetite regulation rather than a merely correlated one.

Leptin represents the endocrine system operating in its long horizon mode, adjusting behavior gradually over days and weeks rather than seconds, in sharp contrast to adrenaline's near instant urgency. It also sets up a natural counterpart, covered in the next chapter, in the hormone ghrelin, which works on a much shorter timescale and points appetite regulation in the opposite direction.
